Population Growth and CO2 Emissions: A Worldwide Analysis

Data management, exploratory analysis, projection and correlation study

MUGISHA Robert | 20252MBI062

06 November 2026

1 Introduction

This report investigates the relationship between population size and CO2 emissions across the countries of the world. Two open datasets are used: the World Population Dataset and the CO2 Emission Around the World dataset (both from Kaggle). The workflow below follows the assignment brief: * data management and cleaning * exploratory data analysis * creation of a new * projected-population variable * visualisation of population * emission trends * correlation / regression study linking population to emissions.

pop_path <- "./data/world_population.csv"
co2_path <- "./data/CO2_emission.csv"

population_raw <- read_csv(pop_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
co2_raw <- read_csv(co2_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

1.2.11 Dealing with missing values and outliers

Missing values. Numeric columns are imputed with the median, which is robust to skew; any missing categorical label is set to "Unknown".

population <- population %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x))) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), "Unknown", .x)))

# confirm no missing values remain
sum(is.na(population))
## [1] 0

Outliers. For this dataset the extreme values in the population columns are genuine (China and India really are an order of magnitude larger than most countries), so they are retained for the ranking tasks. For the rate-type variables used later in the correlation study — density, growth_rate and world_population_percentage — we apply IQR capping (winsorising) so that a handful of extreme territories do not dominate the correlations. The capped copies are stored in new *_capped columns and the originals are left untouched.

cap_iqr <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(.25, .75), na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr <- diff(q)
  lo <- q[1] - 1.5 * iqr
  hi <- q[2] + 1.5 * iqr
  pmin(pmax(x, lo), hi)
}

rate_vars <- intersect(c("density_per_km2", "growth_rate",
                         "world_population_percentage"), names(population))

population <- population %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(rate_vars), cap_iqr, .names = "{.col}_capped"))

glue::glue("Winsorised (IQR-capped) copies created for: ",
           "{paste(rate_vars, collapse = ', ')}.")
## Winsorised (IQR-capped) copies created for: density_per_km2, growth_rate, world_population_percentage.

1.3 Task 4.3 — New variable: projected 2030 population

The exponential population-growth model is

\[N_t = P\,e^{rt},\]

where \(P\) is the present population (end of 2022), \(r\) the growth rate, \(t\) the number of years ahead, and \(e \approx 2.71828\). We project to 2030, so \(t = 2030 - 2022 = 8\).

The raw growth_rate column is inspected first, because the dataset may store it either as an annual factor (values near 1.00), as a fraction (e.g. 0.021) or as a percentage (e.g. 2.1). The code converts whichever form is present into a continuous rate \(r\).

# locate the 2022 population column
pop_2022_col <- names(population)[str_detect(names(population), "2022")][1]
med_gr <- median(population$growth_rate, na.rm = TRUE)

r_vec <- dplyr::case_when(
  med_gr > 0.5 & med_gr < 1.5 ~ population$growth_rate - 1,  # annual factor
  med_gr >= 1.5               ~ population$growth_rate / 100, # percentage
  TRUE                        ~ population$growth_rate        # already a fraction
)

glue::glue("Median raw growth_rate = {round(med_gr, 4)}  ->  ",
           "interpreted as {ifelse(med_gr > 0.5 & med_gr < 1.5, 'annual factor (r = rate - 1)', ifelse(med_gr >= 1.5, 'percentage (r = rate / 100)', 'fraction (r = rate)'))}.")
## Median raw growth_rate = 1.0079  ->  interpreted as annual factor (r = rate - 1).
t_years <- 2030 - 2022

population <- population %>%
  mutate(
    r = r_vec,
    pop_2022 = .data[[pop_2022_col]],
    projected_2030 = round(pop_2022 * exp(r * t_years))
  )

population %>%
  select(country = matches("country"), continent,
         pop_2022, growth_rate, r, projected_2030) %>%
  arrange(desc(pop_2022)) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  kable(caption = "Projected 2030 population (top 10 countries by 2022 population)",
        format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

1.4 Task 4.4 — Top-10 most populous countries: values and plots

1.4.1 4.4.1 Top 10 by 2022 population

country_col <- names(population)[str_detect(names(population), "country_territory")][1]

top10 <- population %>%
  arrange(desc(pop_2022)) %>%
  slice(1:10) %>%
  mutate(country = .data[[country_col]])

top10_names <- top10$country
ggplot(top10, aes(x = reorder(country, pop_2022), y = pop_2022)) +
  geom_col(fill = pal_main) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())(pop_2022)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Top 10 most populous countries, 2022",
       x = NULL, y = "Population (2022)")

1.4.2 4.4.2 Population trend 1990–2022 for the top 10

The population dataset reports census snapshots (1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2022). We reshape those columns to long format and plot the trend.

year_cols <- names(population)[str_detect(names(population), "^x(19|20)\\d{2}_population$")]

trend <- top10 %>%
  select(country, all_of(year_cols)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(year_cols), names_to = "year", values_to = "pop") %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_extract(year, "\\d{4}"))) %>%
  filter(year >= 1990)

ggplot(trend, aes(year, pop, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  labs(title = "Population trend of the 10 most populous countries, 1990–2022",
       x = "Year", y = "Population", colour = NULL)

1.4.3 4.4.3 CO2 emission trend 1990–2019 for the same countries

co2 <- co2_raw %>% clean_names()
co2_year_cols <- names(co2)[str_detect(names(co2), "^x(19|20)\\d{2}")]
co2_country_col <- names(co2)[str_detect(names(co2), "country_name|country$")][1]

co2_long <- co2 %>%
  rename(country = all_of(co2_country_col)) %>%
  select(country, all_of(co2_year_cols)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(co2_year_cols), names_to = "year", values_to = "co2_pc") %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_extract(year, "\\d{4}"))) %>%
  group_by(country, year) %>%
  summarise(co2_pc = mean(co2_pc, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(co2_pc = ifelse(is.nan(co2_pc), NA_real_, co2_pc))

# match the top-10 country names (handles minor naming differences)
name_fix <- c("United States" = "United States",
              "Russia" = "Russian Federation",
              "Egypt" = "Egypt, Arab Rep.")
top10_co2_names <- recode(top10_names, !!!name_fix)

co2_top10 <- co2_long %>%
  filter(country %in% c(top10_names, top10_co2_names),
         year >= 1990, year <= 2019)
ggplot(co2_top10, aes(year, co2_pc, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  labs(title = "CO2 emission trend of the 10 most populous countries, 1990–2019",
       subtitle = "Metric tons per capita",
       x = "Year", y = "CO2 (metric tons per capita)", colour = NULL)

1.5 Task 4.5 — Correlation analysis

1.5.1 4.5.1 Correlations within the population dataset

Correlations between Area, Density, Growth rate and World population percentage (using the IQR-capped rate variables), shown both as a numeric matrix and as a heatmap.

area_col <- names(population)[str_detect(names(population), "area")][1]

corr_df <- population %>%
  transmute(
    Area        = .data[[area_col]],
    Density     = density_per_km2_capped,
    Growth_rate = growth_rate_capped,
    World_pct   = world_population_percentage_capped
  )

corr_mat <- cor(corr_df, use = "complete.obs")
round(corr_mat, 3) %>% kable(caption = "Correlation matrix (population variables)")

Area Density Growth_rate World_pct
Area 1.000 -0.210 -0.013 0.441
Density -0.210 1.000 -0.198 -0.127
Growth_rate -0.013 -0.198 1.000 0.183
World_pct 0.441 -0.127 0.183 1.000 
corrplot(corr_mat, method = "color", type = "upper",
         addCoef.col = "black", tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45,

1.5.2 4.5.2 Population vs CO2 emissions (merged data)

The two datasets are merged on country name; we then keep 2022 population and 2019 CO2 emissions and study the relationship with a scatter plot, correlation coefficients and a simple linear regression.

co2_2019 <- co2_long %>%
  filter(year == 2019) %>%
  select(country, co2_2019 = co2_pc)

pop_small <- population %>%
  transmute(country = .data[[country_col]],
            continent,
            pop_2022,
            projected_2030)

# normalise a few well-known name mismatches before joining
norm_name <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    str_replace_all("United States of America", "United States") %>%
    str_replace_all("Russian Federation", "Russia") %>%
    str_replace_all("Egypt, Arab Rep.", "Egypt") %>%
    str_replace_all("Iran, Islamic Rep.", "Iran") %>%
    str_replace_all("Korea, Rep.", "South Korea") %>%
    str_trim()
}

merged <- pop_small %>%
  mutate(country = norm_name(country)) %>%
  inner_join(co2_2019 %>% mutate(country = norm_name(country)), by = "country") %>%
  filter(!is.na(co2_2019), !is.na(pop_2022))

glue::glue("Countries successfully matched across both datasets: {nrow(merged)}")
## Countries successfully matched across both datasets: 172
ggplot(merged, aes(pop_2022, co2_2019)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = pal_main) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(title = "Population (2022) vs CO2 emissions (2019)",
       subtitle = "Log scale on population; per-capita emissions",
       x = "Population 2022 (log scale)",
       y = "CO2 (metric tons per capita, 2019)")

pear <- cor(merged$pop_2022, merged$co2_2019, method = "pearson")
spear <- cor(merged$pop_2022, merged$co2_2019, method = "spearman")
pear_log <- cor(log10(merged$pop_2022), merged$co2_2019, method = "pearson")

tibble(
  Measure = c("Pearson (raw)", "Spearman (rank)", "Pearson (log population)"),
  Value   = round(c(pear, spear, pear_log), 3)
) %>% kable(caption = "Association between 2022 population and 2019 CO2 per capita")

1.6 Task 4.6 — Comparing CO2 emissions across continents

Using the merged data we sum the 2019 per-capita CO2 emissions within each continent and compare them graphically.

cont_co2 <- merged %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarise(total_co2_2019 = sum(co2_2019, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_countries = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(total_co2_2019))

cont_co2 %>% kable(caption = "Total 2019 CO2 (metric tons per capita) by continent",
                   digits = 2)
Total 2019 CO2 (metric tons per capita) by continent
continent total_co2_2019 n_countries
Asia 261.42 39
Europe 240.97 41
North America 79.57 19
Africa 60.50 49
Oceania 53.20 13
South America 29.42 11 
ggplot(cont_co2, aes(x = reorder(continent, total_co2_2019), y = total_co2_2019)) +
  geom_col(fill = pal_main) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(total_co2_2019, 1)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "Total 2019 CO2 emissions by continent",
       subtitle = "Sum of per-capita values across matched countries",
       x = NULL, y = "Total CO2 (metric tons per capita)")

Answers to the questions (computed from the data):

  1. Highest 2019 CO2 emission: Asia (total 261.42 metric tons per capita).

  2. Third-ranked continent: North America, with a total of 79.57 metric tons per capita.

  3. Lowest-ranked continent: South America, with a total of 29.42 metric tons per capita.

1.7 Conclusion

The analysis cleaned and prepared the World Population Dataset, projected each country’s population to 2030 with the exponential growth model, identified and visualised the ten most populous countries and their population and CO2 trends, and quantified the link between population and per-capita emissions through correlation and regression. The continent comparison summarises where per-capita emissions concentrate. Full narrative discussion, limitations and recommendations are provided in the accompanying LaTeX report.
